questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Factor in the SVD of a Rectangular Matrix
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 4 & 4 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=6$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=4.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 4 & 4 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{8}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 4 & 4 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.
$$

Solving this system, which is equivalent to

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0,\end{aligned}
$$

we get the nonzero normalized solution 

$$
{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $U:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{10}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0.$
Also, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, and we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the second and third columns of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find vectors 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0$ and $‖u‖=1.$

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot u=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{4}{5}{x}_{1}+\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get the general solution 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{4} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}},
$$

where ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables.

Notice that the two linearly independent solutions ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ are mutually orthogonal. Therefore, we only need to normalize them. This gives the second and third columns of $U:$   

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, the matrix $U$ could be the following:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5} & 0 \\ \frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
